title: Undergraduate Application Process & Deadlines
summary: Key deadlines, UCAS application steps, and assessments for applying to Cambridge.
content: To apply to the University of Cambridge as an undergraduate, applicants must submit their UCAS application by 15 October (18:00 UK time) for entry the following autumn. Following the UCAS submission, applicants receive access to My Cambridge Application (formerly SAQ), which must be completed by 22 October. Most applicants must also take a written admission assessment (e.g., ESAT, TMUA, or subject-specific college assessments) either before interview or at interview. Shortlisted candidates are invited for academic interviews in December.

title: Understanding the Cambridge Collegiate System
summary: How colleges function, choosing a college, and open applications.
content: Cambridge is a collegiate university made up of 31 autonomous colleges and 150+ academic departments. The University sets course curricula, organizes central lectures, practicals, and sets and marks examinations, awarding the degrees. Colleges handle admissions, provide student accommodation, meals, social facilities, library resources, pastoral care, and arrange small-group teaching sessions called 'supervisions'. Applicants can select a specific college on UCAS or make an 'open application' which is allocated to a college by an algorithm.

title: Supervisions and Academic Guidance
summary: How supervisions work, Director of Studies, and Tutorial support.
content: Supervisions are the core of Cambridge teaching. They are intensive, weekly or fortnightly teaching sessions typically conducted in groups of one to three students with a specialist supervisor (faculty member or researcher). Students prepare essay work or problem sheets in advance. Every undergraduate is assigned a Director of Studies (DoS) who oversees their academic progress and choices, as well as a College Tutor who provides independent personal and administrative pastoral care.

title: The Cambridge Bursary Scheme & Financial Aid
summary: Non-repayable bursaries, eligibility thresholds, and student hardship funds.
content: The Cambridge Bursary Scheme provides non-repayable annual financial support to eligible Home fee status undergraduate students with household incomes below £62,215. Students with household incomes below £25,000 receive the maximum bursary of up to £3,500 per year (with additional independent student supplements). Financial aid is non-competitive and assessed automatically via Student Finance data. In addition, Colleges and the University operate discretionary Student Hardship Funds for unforeseen financial difficulties.

title: Mental Health, Counselling & Wellbeing Services
summary: University Counselling Service (UCS), College Nurses, and emergency support.
content: Student health and wellbeing support is provided at both college and university levels. Each college has a College Nurse and wellbeing team who can assist with minor illnesses, triage, and pastoral support. The University Counselling Service (UCS) offers free, confidential one-to-one therapy, workshops, and guided self-help for all matriculated students. Students in acute mental health crisis can contact 111 (Option 2 for NHS First Response Service) or reach out to their College Porters' Lodge 24/7.

title: Accessibility and Disability Resource Centre (ADRC)
summary: Support for disabled students, learning difficulties, exam arrangements, and adjustments.
content: The Accessibility and Disability Resource Centre (ADRC) provides confidential advice and confidential Student Support Documents (SSDs) for students with physical disabilities, sensory impairments, chronic health conditions, mental health conditions, and specific learning difficulties (such as dyslexia or ADHD). ADRC helps coordinate academic adjustments, assistive technology, human support (mentors, notetakers), and examination access arrangements (e.g., extra time or rest breaks).

title: Cambridge IT Access, Raven Login & Libraries
summary: University Information Services (UIS), Raven authentication, eduroam, and libraries.
content: All students receive a Cambridge User ID (CRSid) and Raven account credentials upon matriculation. Raven is the single sign-on identity service for accessing Moodle (VLE), Cambridge email, and academic resources. Wi-Fi is accessed via 'eduroam' across the city and university buildings. Cambridge boasts over 100 libraries, including the central Cambridge University Library (a legal deposit library with over 8 million books), faculty libraries, and college libraries open 24/7.

title: Cambridge Careers Service & Handshake Platform
summary: Career counseling, internship fairs, CV reviews, and lifelong alumni services.
content: The Cambridge Careers Service provides guidance to undergraduate and postgraduate students from matriculation through to graduation and beyond. Students can access the Handshake platform for curated job listings, internship schemes, and employer networking events. Services include 1-to-1 career consultations, mock interviews, CV and application reviews, and access to the Cambridge Alumni Mentoring platform.

title: Cambridge Students' Union (Cambridge SU) & Societies
summary: Student representation, clubs, societies directory, and student advice service.
content: The Cambridge Students' Union (Cambridge SU) represents all students across the university and colleges. It runs the Student Advice Service (SAS), providing free, independent, and confidential advocacy on academic appeals, complaints, and disciplinary procedures. Cambridge hosts over 500 clubs and societies covering academic, cultural, political, musical, and sporting interests, including rowing (bumping races), the Cambridge Union debate society, and amateur dramatics (ADC Theatre).
